pools.title: The Comparative Range: Minds Built Nothing Alike
pools.covers: reading §0.1 (claims C2, C3, C4, C7, C12, C14) incl. tbl-same-feats; lecture 0 slides gallery_everyday, gallery_child, gallery_animals, gallery_machines, twenty_watts, the_theme

items.stem: A person, a honeybee, an octopus, and a protein-folding program all do things we are willing to call intelligent, yet the four share almost nothing in what they are physically made of. What does the chapter draw from that fact?

options.text: Whatever explains intelligent behavior cannot be only a fact about the material a system is made of.
options.why: Correct. The argument turns on a mismatch: the behavior is shared and the physical makeup is not, so the explanation has to be pitched somewhere above the level of tissue and silicon. Finding a description that floats free of the material is what the chapter says the field exists to do.

options.text: Intelligent behavior arises only where neurons are present, so the machine cases merely resemble the real thing.
options.why: This is the position the machine examples are chosen to unsettle. The chapter stops short of claiming the programs have minds, but it treats their behavior as real enough that an account resting on neurons alone has a problem to answer.

options.text: Because the four systems differ so sharply, no single science can hold them in view at once.
options.why: This inverts the chapter's conclusion. The diversity is precisely why a description above the level of physical makeup is wanted, and supplying one is what lets a single field study all four side by side.

options.text: The shared behavior points back to a common ancestor whose nervous system all four inherited.
options.why: Common descent does explain shared traits among related organisms, but it cannot reach a protein-folding program, and the chapter's claim concerns the level a description is pitched at rather than lineage.

items.stem: A classmate argues that a program that taught itself to beat the strongest human Go players is not really intelligent, because there are no neurons anywhere in it. Which reply best matches the position the course actually takes?

options.text: The course does not claim the program has a mind, but its behavior troubles any account resting on neurons alone.
options.why: Correct. The claim made about the machine cases is deliberately narrow, and the lecture flags the narrowness out loud: whether such systems have minds is left open as one of the questions the course will work on, while the argument that physical makeup cannot be the whole explanation is treated as hard to dodge.

options.text: The course holds that the Go program has a mind in the same sense a person does, since it solves a hard problem.
options.why: This overclaims in the direction the course is careful to avoid. Solving a hard problem is offered as evidence about what explains intelligent behavior, not as a settled verdict about which systems have minds.

options.text: The course agrees with the classmate: neurons are what make a system intelligent, so machine performance is a separate topic.
options.why: Treating the machine cases as a topic apart is what the course refuses to do. Artificial systems are set up on day one as a running comparison rather than as a category held away from living minds.

options.text: The course sets the question aside as unanswerable, since nobody has directly observed a mind other than their own.
options.why: The difficulty of studying minds from the outside is a real problem the chapter names among the field's driving questions, but naming it is not the same as declining to compare cases, which the chapter does throughout.

items.stem: The lecture showed spectrograms of HOT, HAT, HIT and HEAD spoken by two people. The same word from two speakers looked nothing alike, while different words from a single speaker sometimes looked more similar to each other. What does that finding show about recognizing a spoken word?

options.text: The category the listener recovers is not sitting in the sound as a stable pattern, so the listener must supply it.
options.why: Correct. This is why the demonstration was chosen. If the sound itself carried a reliable signature for HOT, recognition would be a matter of matching; because it does not, recognition has to be something the listener's own machinery constructs.

options.text: Listeners depend on surrounding context rather than the sound, so a word heard in isolation cannot be identified.
options.why: Context certainly helps, but the chapter's companion example cuts against this reading: a single syllable of "hello" from a familiar voice is enough to identify the speaker, with no context at all.

options.text: Spectrograms are too coarse an instrument to display the acoustic features that actually distinguish one vowel from another.
options.why: This blames the instrument for what the demonstration was built to reveal. The variability shown is a genuine property of speech, and it is the reason speech recognition was hard for engineers for so long.

options.text: Speakers unconsciously converge on a shared acoustic target for each word, which is what makes their speech intelligible.
options.why: Convergence of this kind would predict that the same word looks alike across speakers, which is exactly the prediction the spectrograms falsify.

items.stem: Among the animal cases the chapter presents, what is distinctive about the octopus?

options.text: Most of its neurons are threaded through its arms rather than gathered into a central brain.
options.why: Correct. The organization is what makes the case interesting: an octopus solving a problem raises the question of what exactly is doing the solving, since its nervous system is distributed rather than centralized.

options.text: Its whole nervous system holds fewer than a million neurons, far fewer than the task appears to need.
options.why: That description belongs to the honeybee, whose brain the chapter compares to a grain of rice, and whose waggle dance it treats as the striking feat.

options.text: It navigates tens of thousands of miles each year to reach places it has never previously visited.
options.why: Long-distance navigation to unfamiliar feeding grounds is the Arctic tern's feat rather than the octopus's.

options.text: It performs its most impressive feats with no neurons involved in the process at all.
options.why: Having no neurons whatsoever is what sets the artificial systems apart, and it is the basis of the chapter's sharpest version of its argument.

items.stem: The chapter sets the roughly twenty watts a human brain runs on against the power drawn by the machines that fold proteins or master Go. What is that contrast offered to establish?

options.text: A brain achieves feats of this kind on a small fraction of the energy the matching machines require.
options.why: Correct. The comparison is there to make the brain strange again. Eighty-six billion neurons, each in conversation with thousands of others, produce all of this on less power than a household lightbulb, while the machines that rival it on single tasks draw the electricity of a small town.

options.text: Energy efficiency is the property separating a genuine mind from a system that merely imitates one.
options.why: Efficiency is presented as a puzzle worth explaining rather than as a criterion for having a mind, and the chapter is careful not to offer any such criterion this early.

options.text: The brain's low power budget is why it works more slowly than a machine on tasks of similar difficulty.
options.why: No trade-off of this sort is claimed. The point is the opposite one: the brain manages a far wider range of tasks without paying the energy cost the machines pay.

options.text: Machines will match the brain's abilities once their power consumption has been brought down far enough.
options.why: This turns a comparison into a prediction the chapter never makes. Where the machines fall short is treated as an open question rather than as a matter of available electricity.

items.stem: According to the chapter, what makes it remarkable that most young children master the grammar of their native language within a few years?

options.text: They manage it from nothing but the talk around them, with no lessons, no rules, and no correction.
options.why: Correct. The absence of instruction is the whole force of the example. Decades of expensive engineering effort have gone into the same problem, and a small child solves it from ordinary overheard conversation.

options.text: They manage it before the brain regions supporting language have finished developing physically.
options.why: Claims about the maturation of particular brain regions are not what this example rests on, and the chapter makes no argument here about developmental timing in the brain.

options.text: They manage it despite hearing speech that adults have simplified into an incomplete version of the grammar.
options.why: Simplified speech to children is a real phenomenon, but treating it as an obstacle reverses the usual argument, and the chapter's point rests on the absence of teaching rather than the quality of the input.

options.text: They manage it in whatever language surrounds them, which adults learning a second language can no longer do.
options.why: The comparison with adult second-language learning is a genuine topic elsewhere, but the feat highlighted here is learning a first grammar without instruction of any kind.

items.stem: A commentator writes: "A new system composes music that moves people, just as human composers do. That proves the human brain must work the same way this system does." Where does the reasoning go wrong by the chapter's lights?

options.text: Shared behavior across unlike systems shows the material cannot be the whole story, not that mechanisms match.
options.why: Correct. The chapter's argument runs from shared behavior to a constraint on what an explanation must look like. Reading it as an identity claim about mechanisms gets it backwards, since the same behavior turning up in a bee, an octopus and a machine is evidence that very different mechanisms can produce it.

options.text: Music is an aesthetic matter rather than a cognitive one, so the case falls outside what the field actually studies.
options.why: The field's scope is drawn much more widely than this, and the chapter treats capacities from navigation to humor to protein folding as fair game.

options.text: Machines cannot move people emotionally, so the premise fails before the conclusion is even reached.
options.why: Whether the effect is genuine is not the flaw being probed here, and the chapter is willing to grant that artificial systems produce apt and impressive results.

options.text: Nothing follows from one case, and the argument would go through if enough composing systems were compared.
options.why: Adding cases would not repair it. The problem is the shape of the inference rather than the size of the sample, since more matches would still not show that the mechanisms are the same.

items.stem: In lecture, a picture of sliced oranges was shown, and some students noticed they had become a little hungry. The lecture flagged this as a preview of a deep question. Which question was it?

options.text: Why identifying an object should come bundled with wanting it, rather than the two being separate matters.
options.why: Correct. Recognition arriving already tied to an appraisal is a real puzzle about what minds are for, and the course takes it up directly when it reaches how nervous systems work out whether something is good or bad.

options.text: Why a picture of an object produces much the same bodily response that the object itself would produce.
options.why: Responses to depictions are an interesting topic in their own right, but the puzzle raised was about recognition and wanting arriving together rather than about pictures standing in for objects.

options.text: Why some categories of object are recognized faster than others when they are seen only briefly.
options.why: Differences in recognition speed across categories belong to the study of pattern recognition, which the course reaches much later and for different reasons.

options.text: Why people can recognize an object from a photograph they have never seen before, or from an angle they have not seen.
options.why: Generalizing to a never-before-seen instance is a genuine puzzle the course takes up, and the spectrogram demonstration in the same lecture makes the point for speech.

items.stem: The chapter opens by pointing out that its first sentence has in all likelihood never been produced before, and yet the reader understands it effortlessly. What does that observation establish?

options.text: Understanding cannot work by retrieving a stored meaning, since a novel sentence has none to retrieve.
options.why: Correct. Novelty is what rules out the simplest account. Whatever the reader is doing has to build a meaning from an arrangement encountered for the first time, which is a far harder thing than looking one up.

options.text: Understanding depends on the reader having encountered every individual word in the sentence before.
options.why: Familiar words are necessary but nowhere near sufficient, and the observation is aimed at the arrangement rather than at the vocabulary.

options.text: Written language is processed differently from speech, since only writing produces genuinely novel sentences.
options.why: Novelty is a property of ordinary speech as much as of writing, and the chapter treats ink marks and air vibrations in the same breath as two routes to the same accomplishment.

options.text: Comprehension is slower for unfamiliar sentences, which is why careful reading takes deliberate effort.
options.why: The striking thing about the example is the absence of effort, and the chapter emphasizes that the reader takes the sentence in with no sense of working at it.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain why the range of cases in this module — a person, a honeybee, an octopus, and a program with no neurons at all — makes trouble for any explanation of intelligence pitched at the level of what a system is physically made of. Say what kind of description the chapter proposes reaching for instead.
items.answer: Each of these systems does something we are willing to call intelligent: a person understands a sentence never spoken before, a bee communicates the direction and distance of flowers, an octopus works out a jar, a program predicts how a protein folds. But they are made of almost nothing in common — three pounds of tissue, a brain the size of a grain of rice, neurons distributed through eight arms, and silicon. So an explanation given in terms of the material cannot cover all four, because there is no shared material to appeal to. What the chapter proposes instead is a description of what a mind is doing that floats free of what it is made of, pitched at the level of information and process rather than tissue. That is the description the field calls computational, and having one is what makes it possible to study these cases side by side as instances of a single subject.
rubric: Names at least two of the cases and says, for each, what it does that counts as intelligent.
States plainly that the systems share almost nothing physically.
Draws the conclusion that an explanation in terms of physical makeup cannot cover all the cases at once.
Says the alternative is a description pitched above the material, in terms of information and process.
Connects that description to why one field can study these cases together.

items.stem: The chapter's table of four systems that do intelligent things counts neurons for the human, the bee and the octopus, but measures the AI model in parameters and its appetite as "a warehouse of computers" — and leaves the bee's and the octopus's power cells blank. What does the table's refusal to fill every cell with a comparable number show?

options.text: The systems differ so deeply that even the units of measurement do not carry across from one to the next.
options.why: Correct. The blanks are the honest part. No power figure exists for a nervous system on its own, and parameters are not neurons under another name. When the yardsticks themselves fail to line up, the claim that these systems share almost nothing lands harder than any list of differing numbers would.

options.text: Measurements of invertebrate nervous systems are unreliable, so the chapter withholds the figures it cannot properly trust.
options.why: Reliability is not the issue: the table does give counts for both the bee and the octopus, and its sourcing record traces each to a published study. What it omits is power, which nobody has measured for a nervous system alone.

options.text: The chapter treats artificial systems as a separate category that its comparison is not really meant to include.
options.why: Artificial systems are the opposite of excluded. The argument needs a case with no neurons at all, and the table's last row is exactly where that case sits.

options.text: Neuron counts predict capability poorly, so the chapter avoids implying that more neurons would mean more intelligence.
options.why: Whether counts predict capability is a real question, and one the octopus quietly complicates, but the blanks are about measurements nobody has made rather than about an inference the chapter declines to draw.

items.stem: A student objects that the opening feats — understanding a sentence nobody has spoken before, knowing a friend from a single "hello" — cannot really be hard, since we do them constantly and without noticing. How does the chapter answer that?

options.text: Performing a thing endlessly and without effort hides its difficulty; it is no evidence that it is easy.
options.why: Correct. The chapter separates two things that ordinarily travel together: how hard a problem is, and how hard it feels. These feats outran the best engineering for most of human history while costing an ordinary person nothing, and that gap is where the field lives.

options.text: The feats are easy for people and hard for machines, so how hard something is depends on which kind of system attempts it.
options.why: This makes difficulty relative to the system, which runs against the chapter's point. The problems are hard in their own right, and it is the human case that stands in need of explaining.

options.text: They only feel effortless through practice, and any sufficiently practised skill eventually becomes automatic.
options.why: Practice does automatize skills, but the chapter's lead example is understanding a sentence that has never been produced before, which nobody can have practised.

options.text: Each feat is fairly simple on its own and seems impressive only when many of them are listed together.
options.why: The chapter dwells on single cases — one syllable, one sentence — precisely because each is meant to be remarkable alone rather than by accumulation.

items.stem: Having set the human, animal and machine feats side by side, the chapter says the two smallest and hardest questions to ask are how? and why? What does asking both, rather than either one, commit the field to?

options.text: An account of by what means an ability works still owes a separate answer about what it is for.
options.why: Correct. The two questions come apart: a complete story about the machinery leaves the question of what the machinery is for untouched, and a good answer about purpose explains nothing about mechanism. The course is built on keeping both open at once.

options.text: An account of the mechanism, once complete, will contain the answer about purpose as one of its consequences.
options.why: This collapses the pair into one question, which is the move the chapter is guarding against by naming two.

options.text: An account must choose between the two, since a mechanistic answer and a purposive one cannot both be correct.
options.why: Neither question is offered as ruling out the other; the chapter treats them as two things to ask about one system.

options.text: An account of purpose has to come first, because a mechanism cannot be described until its goal is known.
options.why: No priority of that kind is claimed here, and the chapter asks both questions of every case without ordering them.

items.stem: The opening section closes by asking whether brain and cognitive science is "really one subject, or a loose collection of older disciplines that only happen to overlap." What is the standing of that question at this point?

options.text: Genuinely open, and deliberately left unsettled here rather than answered.
options.why: Correct. The chapter raises the doubt about its own field on purpose and hands it forward. Taking a position on it is the work of the section that follows, and the answer there is careful rather than reassuring.

options.text: Rhetorical: the chapter has just demonstrated the field's unity and is inviting the reader to agree.
options.why: Nothing before this point argues for unity. What has been shown is a range of systems and a range of researchers, which is what makes the question worth asking.

options.text: Settled in the negative: the chapter's considered position is that these remain separate disciplines with no real unity.
options.why: The chapter is honest about how disconnected the disciplines are, but it treats their unity as a wager worth making rather than one already lost.

options.text: A matter of academic administration rather than a substantive question about the subject.
options.why: The question is substantive for this book, since whether these inquiries are facets of one subject is what would justify studying them together at all.

items.stem: What is brain and cognitive science, as this book uses the term?

options.text: The interdisciplinary, computational study of the mind and brain, across humans, animals and machines.
options.why: Correct. Both adjectives carry weight. Interdisciplinary, because no one field's tools reach everything that shapes a mind; computational, because that is the description that fits a person, a bee and a machine at once.

options.text: The branch of neuroscience that works out how particular brain structures give rise to thought and behavior.
options.why: This describes roughly what neuroscience contributes, which the book treats as one discipline among several rather than as the whole enterprise.

options.text: The engineering discipline concerned with building machines that reproduce human reasoning and perception.
options.why: That is close to artificial intelligence, which the book counts as one of the contributing fields and as a source of comparisons.

options.text: The philosophical study of how mental states are related to physical states of the body.
options.why: The mind–body relation is a question the book takes up, and philosophy is one of the disciplines it draws on, but neither is the field as a whole.

items.stem: Which term does this book use for the interdisciplinary, computational study of the mind — the enterprise that gathers the questions asked about human, animal and artificial minds under one name?

options.text: brain and cognitive science
options.why: Correct. The name is doing work the book is explicit about: it gathers questions that grew up in separate disciplines, and asserts that they are questions about one subject.

options.text: cognitive psychology
options.why: One of the contributing disciplines, and the one asking what operations the mind performs — a part of the enterprise rather than the whole of it.

options.text: computer science and artificial intelligence
options.why: Another contributing discipline, named this way in the chapter's own roster, and a running source of comparisons — but one lens among several rather than the whole.

options.text: levels of analysis
options.why: The frame that sorts the field's questions into kinds. It organizes the enterprise; it is not a name for it.

items.stem: The chapter claims that our own cognitive feats go unnoticed because they are performed constantly and without effort, not because they are simple. In a short paragraph, explain the distinction being drawn, and say why the chapter chooses to open on ordinary experience rather than on a laboratory finding.
items.answer: The chapter separates how hard a problem actually is from how hard it feels to the person solving it. Understanding a sentence, recognizing a voice, and reading a scene are all effortless from the inside, and that effortlessness is exactly what hides their difficulty — we notice the things we struggle with, so a capacity that never fails never draws attention. The evidence that these are hard problems comes from elsewhere: they defeated the best engineering for most of human history, and some of them are still not reliably solved. Opening on ordinary experience puts the reader's own mind in the position of the thing to be explained, which a laboratory result could not do. It also makes the field's central puzzle available before any technical vocabulary has been introduced, so the reader feels the question before being handed the machinery for answering it.
rubric: Distinguishes the difficulty of a problem from the felt effort of solving it.
Says that constancy and effortlessness are what conceal the difficulty, rather than evidence of simplicity.
Gives at least one of the chapter's examples of an effortless-but-hard feat.
Points to evidence of difficulty from outside introspection — that these problems resisted engineering, or remain unsolved.
Gives a reason for opening on the reader's own experience: it makes the reader the case to be explained, or raises the puzzle before any vocabulary exists for it.

pools.title: What Brain and Cognitive Science Is
pools.covers: reading §0.2 (claims C1, C2, C3, C4, C5, C6, C8, C9, C10, C12); lecture 0 slide the_journey

items.stem: This section opens by returning to the feats from the previous one — the sentence understood, the bird's navigation, the folded protein, the twenty-watt brain. What does it use them to establish this time?

options.text: Each is studied by people trained in a different tradition, so no single science owns the whole set.
options.why: Correct. The same examples do different work in each section. In the opening they showed that intelligent behavior turns up in systems built nothing alike; here they show that the study of those abilities is as scattered as the abilities are varied, which is the problem the rest of the section takes up.

options.text: Intelligent behavior turns up in systems that share almost nothing in what they are physically made of.
options.why: That is what these examples established the first time. Reusing them here is deliberate, but the point now being drawn is about the researchers rather than the systems.

options.text: The abilities are more closely related to one another than the variety of the examples suggests.
options.why: No such convergence is claimed. The examples stay as varied as they were, and what gathers them is a set of questions rather than a shared mechanism.

options.text: Ordinary people perform these feats constantly and without any sense of effort or difficulty.
options.why: True of several of them, and the reason the chapter opened on them, but effortlessness is not what this passage draws attention to.

items.stem: A researcher studies how a species' capacity for tool use changed over many generations, rather than how one animal's skill develops during its own life. Does that fall inside the chapter's working definition of brain and cognitive science?

options.text: Yes: the definition covers minds coming to be over a lifetime and across generations.
options.why: Correct. The working definition is deliberately wide on exactly this axis. Development within a life and change across generations are named as two timescales of one question, which is what lets the evolutionary thread run through the whole book.

options.text: No: change across generations belongs to evolutionary biology rather than to this field.
options.why: Evolutionary biology is one of the contributing disciplines rather than a neighbor the field hands work to, and the chapter names deep time explicitly.

options.text: No: the definition is restricted to how minds and brains work, not to how they came about.
options.why: How minds and brains come to be is stated in the definition alongside how they work, in the same sentence.

options.text: Yes, but because tool use is a behavior, and behavior is what the field ultimately studies.
options.why: The definition is not narrowed to behavior; it reaches minds, brains, and their consequences, across organisms and artificial systems alike.

items.stem: The chapter says brain and cognitive science is best understood not as a finished, unified field but as an aspiration. On what grounds?

options.text: The disciplines grew up apart and stay disconnected in practice, so the unity is a bet.
options.why: Correct. The evidence offered is about working life rather than about theory: separate traditions, separate journals, and researchers who can study one capacity for years without reading each other. The aspiration is the claim that these are nonetheless facets of one subject.

options.text: The field is too young to have settled on the methods and standards a mature science needs.
options.why: Youth is not the argument, and several of the contributing disciplines are old. What is new is the proposal to treat their questions as one subject.

options.text: Its central questions are so large that no one expects them to be answered in the foreseeable future.
options.why: The chapter is candid about hard questions, but difficulty is a separate matter from whether the enterprise is one field.

options.text: Most researchers whose work bears on the mind reject the idea that a unified field is possible.
options.why: No such rejection is reported. The chapter's point is milder and stranger: many of them have simply never had occasion to think about it.

items.stem: A student reads that brain and cognitive science is "an aspiration" and concludes that the chapter does not take the field seriously. Where does the reasoning go wrong?

options.text: Calling the unity a bet describes where the field stands, and the book makes that bet.
options.why: Correct. The honesty and the commitment are the same move. The chapter states plainly how disconnected the disciplines are and then says the wager is worth making — and organizes every chapter that follows as though it were.

options.text: The chapter is being modest for effect, and its real position is that the field is already unified.
options.why: Nothing is being softened for effect. The disconnection described is presented as a genuine feature of how the work is done.

options.text: Whether the field is unified is a question about institutions, so it says nothing about the subject.
options.why: Whether these scattered questions are facets of one subject is exactly what would justify pursuing them together, which makes it substantive rather than administrative.

options.text: The chapter takes no position, leaving the reader to decide whether the field holds together.
options.why: A position is taken and acted on. The wager is named as a wager and then the book is arranged around having accepted it.

items.stem: The chapter says this book does not give each discipline its own chapter — philosophy here, neuroscience there, linguistics and artificial intelligence off on their own. What is the alternative it describes?

options.text: Two threads: the order evolution added the capacities, and living minds set beside machine ones.
options.why: Correct. Both threads are meant to do the weaving that a discipline-per-chapter structure cannot. Each capacity is met in roughly the order it arrived, and each is set beside whatever the machine version of it looks like.

options.text: Each chapter takes one discipline's methods and applies them to a capacity chosen to suit those methods.
options.why: This keeps the discipline as the organizing unit and merely varies the topic, which is the arrangement the chapter is rejecting.

options.text: The chapters follow the history of the field, from its philosophical origins to its computational present.
options.why: A history of the field is not the organizing principle; the order the chapters follow is the order in which the capacities themselves arose.

options.text: The chapters are arranged by the part of the brain that carries out the capacity under discussion.
options.why: Anatomy is not the spine of the book. Organizing by brain region would also sit oddly with a book that keeps machines in view throughout.

items.stem: Introducing the evolutionary thread, the chapter says it "is no longer the loose guesswork it once was." What objection is it answering, and how?

options.text: That evolutionary explanation is storytelling after the fact, answered by pointing to the evidence.
options.why: Correct. The worry is real and old: an evolutionary account can be invented to fit any trait, which makes it unfalsifiable and therefore idle. The reply is not that the worry is silly but that the field has changed, and its claims now rest on evidence rather than on plausibility.

options.text: That evolution works far too slowly to explain capacities that appear within a single human lifetime.
options.why: Timescales are not in dispute here. The chapter treats development and evolution as two separate questions rather than as rivals.

options.text: That evolutionary claims about the mind cannot be tested because minds leave no fossils.
options.why: The absence of fossilized behavior is a genuine methodological problem, but the sentence is answering the charge of storytelling rather than one about preservation.

options.text: That focusing on evolution would crowd out the comparison with artificial systems.
options.why: The two threads are presented as complementary and run alongside each other, so no crowding-out is contemplated.

items.stem: The chapter introduces two commitments and calls them "better read as the ideals this book pursues than as a consensus that already exists." What is that qualification doing?

options.text: Marking them as positions this book adopts and argues for, not agreement the field has reached.
options.why: Correct. The qualification matches the honesty of the aspiration framing a paragraph earlier. The reader is told which claims are the book's own before those claims start doing work, which is what makes the following two sections arguments rather than reports.

options.text: Warning that the commitments are provisional and may well be abandoned later in the book.
options.why: Nothing signals that either commitment is temporary. Both organize the rest of the book and are defended rather than dropped.

options.text: Indicating that they are goals for the field to reach rather than claims that could be true or false.
options.why: They are treated as claims throughout, argued for in the two sections that follow, and weighed against objections.

options.text: Conceding that most researchers who study the mind would reject both commitments.
options.why: No such rejection is reported. What the chapter reports is disconnection between disciplines, which is a different thing from disagreement.

items.stem: The chapter gives a reason that a computational description, in particular, could serve as the language all these disciplines share. What is the reason?

options.text: A description pitched at information and process sits above the level of cells and silicon.
options.why: Correct. The argument runs directly from the opening section. A human, a bee, an octopus and a machine share nothing in material, so any description that mentions material fits only one of them; a description that does not mention it can fit all four.

options.text: All four kinds of system turn out to process information in fundamentally the same way.
options.why: Far more than the chapter claims. What they share is that each takes in information and does something with it, not that they do it alike.

options.text: Computation is the only description precise enough to state a theory of the mind at all.
options.why: Precision is offered later as one benefit of the computational description, but it is not what makes the vocabulary shareable across such different systems.

options.text: Any of these systems can in principle be simulated on a computer, which puts them on common ground.
options.why: Simulability is a different claim, and one the chapter does not make here. The point concerns the level a description is pitched at.

items.stem: The chapter describes a neuroscientist tracing serotonin's effect on firing rate, a psychologist asking what sways people's choices, a developmental geneticist studying how genes build brain structures, a linguist and a computer scientist building a conversational program, and a philosopher asking whether a pig's mind bears on how we treat it. What are these five offered to show?

options.text: That these are genuinely different jobs rather than variations on a single one.
options.why: Correct. The chapter lands the point in a phrase worth remembering: different jobs, in different buildings, with different tools and different journals. The vignettes are there to make the diversity concrete before the question of unity is raised.

options.text: That the mind can be studied at many levels, from the molecular up to the social.
options.why: A tidy summary, and roughly true, but the levels framing arrives later and is not what these five are illustrating.

options.text: That every one of these researchers would describe themselves as a cognitive scientist.
options.why: The chapter says close to the opposite: many have never used the label and some may not have met it.

options.text: That the disciplines have converged on a shared set of methods for studying the mind.
options.why: The vignettes are chosen for how little the methods have in common, which is what makes the disconnection vivid.

items.stem: Why does the chapter treat the last decade's progress in artificial intelligence as useful to a book about minds?

options.text: Each working system that sees, converses, plans or learns is a fresh point of comparison.
options.why: Correct. The value is comparative rather than substitutive. Every new working system sharpens questions that were already being asked about living minds, and raises some that could not have been asked before it existed.

options.text: Artificial systems have reached the point where they can be treated as minds in their own right.
options.why: That question is deliberately left open. The usefulness claimed here does not depend on how it is eventually answered.

options.text: Studying artificial systems is easier and cheaper than studying animals or people directly.
options.why: Convenience is not the argument, and nothing suggests the machine cases are meant to replace the living ones.

options.text: Progress in artificial intelligence has settled several long-standing disputes about how minds work.
options.why: The chapter says these systems sharpen old questions and raise new ones, which is some distance from settling anything.

items.stem: A student objects that since cognitive science departments, journals and conferences plainly exist, the field must already be unified. How does the chapter's account complicate that?

options.text: The label can exist while the fields it gathers stay disconnected in daily practice.
options.why: Correct. The test the chapter applies is what researchers actually do, not what the sign on the building says. Its example is pointed: a linguist and a neuroscientist can work on the same capacity for years without reading each other's papers.

options.text: Those institutions are recent, and too new for their effects on research practice to have appeared.
options.why: Their age is not discussed, and the disconnection described is presented as a current fact rather than a lag.

options.text: The institutions exist but admit only researchers already committed to a computational view.
options.why: No such gatekeeping is described, and the chapter presents the computational commitment as the book's own rather than an entry requirement.

options.text: Most researchers who use the label mean something different by it from what this book means.
options.why: Disagreement over the term's meaning is not the issue raised; many of the researchers in question never reach for the term at all.

items.stem: In lecture, having laid out the semester as the order evolution added things, the instructor said the same question is asked every single week: what problem did this capacity solve for the creature that first had it. What did he say that repeated question accomplishes?

options.text: It makes the course one story rather than fifteen disconnected topics.
options.why: Correct. The claim is about coherence, and it is what the evolutionary ordering is for. Without a question asked of every capacity the sequence would be a list; with one, each week is a further instalment of a single argument.

options.text: It keeps every week's material tied to evidence from the fossil and comparative record.
options.why: Evidence was not the point being made. The question was offered as what holds the weeks together, whatever evidence eventually answers it.

options.text: It ensures that each capacity is examined at all three levels of analysis in turn.
options.why: The three levels are the frame for working through a capacity, but they are a separate device from the question asked of every week.

options.text: It guarantees the capacities are covered in the order a student will find easiest.
options.why: The order is the order the capacities arose in, which is not chosen for ease and sometimes cuts against it.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain what the chapter means by calling brain and cognitive science a "wager," and say how taking that wager seriously shapes the way this book is organized.
items.answer: The wager is the claim that questions which grew up in separate disciplines — how neurons carry information, why people choose as they do, what structure lets a child speak — are really facets of one subject, and are better pursued together than apart. The chapter calls it a wager rather than a fact because the disciplines mostly grew up apart and stay disconnected in practice: many researchers never use the label, and a linguist and a neuroscientist can work on the same capacity for years without reading each other. Taking the bet seriously is what rules out the obvious structure, a chapter per discipline, since that arrangement would simply reproduce the separation the wager denies. Instead two threads run through every chapter: the capacities are met roughly in the order evolution added them, each introduced by asking what problem it solved, and each is set beside its artificial counterpart. Underneath both threads sit the two commitments — that no one discipline can explain a mind alone, and that computation is what lets the disciplines speak — which the chapter is careful to present as the book's own position rather than settled agreement.
rubric: States the wager as the claim that questions from separate disciplines are facets of one subject.
Gives the reason it is called a wager rather than a fact — the disciplines grew up apart and remain disconnected in practice.
Says that a chapter-per-discipline structure is rejected, and connects the rejection to the wager.
Names at least one of the two organizing threads, evolutionary order or natural against artificial.
Notes that the two commitments are presented as the book's own position rather than as existing consensus.

pools.title: The Disciplines, and the Question Each Asks
pools.covers: reading §0.3 (claims C1–C8, C12, C14, C15) incl. tbl-disciplines; lecture 0 slide same_mind_different_questions

items.stem: The chapter says a mind is shaped by cells and chemistry, brain structure, evolutionary history, individual development, language, and culture. What conclusion does it draw from that list?

options.text: No one field's tools reach all of them, so a science of the mind has to be interdisciplinary.
options.why: Correct. The argument is about reach rather than about goodwill. Each of those forces has a discipline built around it, with methods suited to that force and to little else, so a science that wants all six has no option but to be a collection of lenses.

options.text: Each of those forces contributes about equally to a mind, so no one of them should be studied before the others.
options.why: No claim about equal weighting is made, and the chapter never suggests the forces have to be taken in any particular order.

options.text: The list is so long that no science can handle it, so real progress must wait for better methods.
options.why: The chapter draws the opposite conclusion. The length of the list is why several fields are needed at once, not a reason to expect the work to stall.

options.text: The forces interact so tightly that dividing them among separate disciplines was a mistake from the start.
options.why: The separation is treated as a historical fact with a reason behind it — each field grew up around one force — rather than as an error to be undone.

items.stem: What does it mean to call a field interdisciplinary, in the sense this chapter uses?

options.text: It draws on many different disciplines at once, because no one of them can explain its subject alone.
options.why: Correct. The definition has two halves and the second is what gives the first its force. Drawing on several fields is not a matter of breadth for its own sake; it follows from the claim that no single field's tools reach everything that shapes a mind.

options.text: It sits in the gap between two established disciplines, studying what neither of them covers.
options.why: That describes a field defined by a gap, which is a real way for disciplines to form but not what is meant here — the fields in question all study the mind, and none is left over.

options.text: It borrows methods freely from other fields while keeping its own questions and its own standards.
options.why: Method-borrowing happens constantly and is not the point. What is claimed is that the questions belong to several fields at once, not that one field shops for techniques.

options.text: Its researchers are each trained across several disciplines rather than specializing in any one of them.
options.why: The chapter describes the opposite situation: researchers trained in one tradition, in different buildings with different journals, whose questions nonetheless need each other.

items.stem: Which term does this book use for a field that draws on many different disciplines at once, because no single one of them can explain its subject alone?

options.text: interdisciplinary
options.why: Correct. It is the first of the book's two commitments about brain and cognitive science, and the one this section spends its length arguing for.

options.text: integration
options.why: The word the chapter uses for the right relationship among the disciplines, as against a ranking. It names how they should stand to each other rather than the property of the field.

options.text: computation
options.why: The second commitment, and the answer to a different question: what lets these disciplines speak to one another once they are gathered.

options.text: levels of analysis
options.why: The frame that sorts the field's questions into kinds. It comes later, and it organizes the questions rather than describing the field's makeup.

items.stem: Having walked through eight disciplines, the chapter says something about what actually changed from one to the next. What was it?

options.text: The subject stayed the same throughout, and what changed was the question each field brought to it.
options.why: Correct. This is the section's payoff and the insight the whole course is arranged on. Every one of the eight studies minds; what separates them is which question they think worth asking about one.

options.text: The subject narrowed steadily at each step, from whole societies down to individual cells.
options.why: The disciplines are not presented in any such order, and the chapter's list moves between scales freely rather than descending through them.

options.text: The methods changed little, even though each field describes them in its own vocabulary.
options.why: Methods differ enormously between these fields — different tools, different journals — which the previous section made vivid with its five practitioner vignettes.

options.text: The questions stayed largely constant while the answers each discipline offered steadily diverged.
options.why: This reverses the claim exactly. It is the questions that differ; on the subject they are all asking about, the fields agree.

items.stem: A student concludes that since brains are made of neurons, neuroscience must be the real science of the mind, and the other fields are placeholders until it catches up. What does the chapter say against that?

options.text: Each field answers a question the others need answered, so the relation is integration.
options.why: Correct. The reply is not that neuroscience matters less, but that a ranking mistakes the situation. A psychologist's account of what operation is performed is something a neuroscientist needs in order to know what to look for, and the dependence runs in every direction.

options.text: Neuroscience is among the youngest of these disciplines and has not yet earned any such standing.
options.why: Relative age is not the argument, and it would be a weak one — the ranking would simply be granted later rather than now.

options.text: Neurons are not really what a mind is made of, so the argument fails before it can get started.
options.why: The chapter does not deny that minds are made of neurons. It denies that being the material settles which description explains best.

options.text: The other fields study altogether different subjects, so no ranking among them would be possible.
options.why: The section's whole point is that they study the same subject. If they studied different things the ranking question would not arise at all.

items.stem: The chapter offers an explanation for why researchers in these fields so often talk past one another. What is it?

options.text: They ask different questions about one subject, and the difference usually goes unstated.
options.why: Correct. The failure is not that anyone is wrong but that two people can answer a question each and be answering different ones, while both believe the topic is the same. Naming the difference is what turns the impasse into a division of labor.

options.text: Their vocabularies have drifted so far apart that the same words now mean quite different things.
options.why: Divergent vocabulary is real and the chapter notices it, but it is treated as a further obstacle rather than as the root of the trouble.

options.text: They work from incompatible assumptions about whether the mind can be studied scientifically at all.
options.why: Whether the mind can be studied is a question the chapter raises elsewhere; it is not what is said to divide these particular fields from one another.

options.text: They compete for the same funding and the same readership, which discourages real engagement.
options.why: Competition of that kind is not mentioned, and the disconnection described is the milder one of simply never reading each other's work.

items.stem: After the tour of disciplines the chapter notes that their questions "fall into a small number of recurring kinds." What does it say that makes possible?

options.text: Organizing a course around the questions themselves rather than teaching each field in its own box.
options.why: Correct. It is the quiet setup for what comes later. If the questions reduced to nothing but eight disciplinary habits there would be no alternative to a chapter apiece; because they fall into kinds, the kinds can become the structure.

options.text: Ranking the questions according to how fundamental each is to any explanation of a mind.
options.why: Ranking is precisely what the section has just argued against, and it argues against ranking questions for the same reason it argues against ranking fields.

options.text: Assigning each discipline its own stage in the order a full explanation has to be built up.
options.why: No such sequence is proposed. The kinds of question are not stages that follow one another but different things to ask about the same system.

options.text: Reducing the eight disciplines down to the three or four that ask genuinely distinct questions.
options.why: Nothing is being eliminated. All eight keep their questions; what is claimed is that those questions fall into families.

items.stem: Both neuroscience and cognitive psychology study how a person recognizes a friend's voice. How does the chapter distinguish the questions they bring to it?

options.text: Neuroscience asks about the physical machinery; cognitive psychology asks what operations it performs.
options.why: Correct. The pair is the clearest case of the section's claim. Which pathway carries the sound, and what is held onto between hearing and knowing, are questions about one event that neither field's methods could answer for the other.

options.text: Neuroscience studies the brain, while cognitive psychology studies observable behavior and nothing else.
options.why: That characterization fits radical behaviorism rather than cognitive psychology, which is defined here by its interest in the representations and processes behind behavior.

options.text: Neuroscience works mainly with animal subjects while cognitive psychology works mainly with people.
options.why: Typical subject populations are not what the chapter uses to tell the fields apart, and both study humans extensively.

options.text: Neuroscience explains the capacity, while cognitive psychology can do no more than describe it.
options.why: This is the ranking the section rejects, dressed as a distinction. Both fields explain; they explain answers to different questions.

items.stem: The chapter sets philosophy apart from the other seven, saying it does something they cannot easily do for themselves. What is that?

options.text: It asks whether the questions the other fields are asking are well posed in the first place.
options.why: Correct. The work described is prior to any finding: sharpening loose concepts, dragging hidden assumptions into the open, and testing whether a claim is coherent enough to be worth the effort of investigating.

options.text: It settles the disputes that arise between other fields when their findings come into conflict.
options.why: Philosophy is not cast as an arbiter over the others. Its job is with the questions rather than with adjudicating answers.

options.text: It supplies the definitions of mind and thought that all the other fields then work with.
options.why: Sharpening concepts is part of the description, but the chapter does not have the other fields waiting on definitions handed down to them.

options.text: It studies the mind directly, without depending on any evidence from the other seven fields.
options.why: Independence of that kind is not claimed, and philosophy is presented as one lens among the collection rather than as a self-sufficient one.

items.stem: In the chapter's table every discipline is put to one and the same moment: recognizing a friend from a single "hello." One row asks which differences between voices a community treats as meaningful, and which it never hears. Whose row is that?

options.text: Anthropology, which asks how the society a mind grows up in shapes what that mind can do.
options.why: Correct. Culture is the force the chapter says biology leaves out, and the row follows from it directly: which vocal differences a community has learned to hear is a fact about that community rather than about ears.

options.text: Linguistics, which asks what hidden structure lets a person speak and understand at all.
options.why: Linguistics has its own row, asking how a single syllable manages to carry a word and an identity at once.

options.text: Education, which asks how minds actually learn, and what teaching them reveals about them.
options.why: Education's row asks how a child comes to tell familiar voices apart, and whether that can be taught.

options.text: Cognitive psychology, which asks what operations the machinery of the mind actually performs.
options.why: Cognitive psychology's row asks what is held onto between hearing and knowing, and what turns the one into the other.

items.stem: The chapter's table of disciplines gives every row the same capacity — recognizing a friend from one "hello" — rather than a different example for each. What does holding the example fixed let the table show?

options.text: That the subject is what stays constant while the question varies from row to row.
options.why: Correct. Giving each discipline its own example would have made the table a list of what different fields happen to work on. Holding one moment still turns the same table into an argument, because the only thing left free to vary is the question.

options.text: That every one of these disciplines could in principle study any capacity a mind has.
options.why: Probably true, and not what the table is arranged to demonstrate. Its work is done by what stays fixed rather than by what could be substituted.

options.text: That recognizing a voice is the capacity best suited to genuinely interdisciplinary study.
options.why: The example is chosen because it is ordinary and already familiar from the opening section, not because it is uniquely well suited to being shared.

options.text: That the disciplines produce answers that can be laid side by side and directly compared.
options.why: Comparable answers would need a shared vocabulary, which is the problem the section hands forward rather than one it has solved.

items.stem: In lecture, five researchers were shown looking at the same three-year-old who says "I goed to the store." What did the instructor say stays the same across all five, and what changes?

options.text: The subject stays the same, one child and one mistake, and only the question changes.
options.why: Correct. The example was given as a second version of the same point the chapter makes with a friend calling your name — worth having twice, the instructor said, because it is the key to the entire enterprise.

options.text: The question stays the same, and only the method each field brings to it changes.
options.why: This inverts the point. Shared methods are what these fields conspicuously lack; what they share is the child.

options.text: The methods stay much the same, while the vocabulary each field uses to describe them differs.
options.why: A neuroscientist, a linguist and an AI researcher approaching one child would not share methods, and nothing in the example suggests they would.

options.text: The evidence stays the same, and each of the five draws a quite different conclusion from it.
options.why: The five are not shown disagreeing. Each asks something the others are not asking, which is a different situation from reaching conflicting conclusions.

items.stem: In lecture the instructor said the three-year-old's "goed" is a mistake worth dwelling on. What did he say the error is evidence of?

options.text: Something she built herself: nobody said "goed" to her, so she cannot have copied it.
options.why: Correct. That is what makes the error more revealing than a correct form would be. A right answer might have been memorized; a wrong one that appears in nobody's speech has to have been produced by a rule she worked out and then applied where it does not hold.

options.text: A gap in what she has so far heard, which more exposure to adult speech will eventually fill.
options.why: Exposure is not what is missing. She has heard "went" many times; the error comes from something she has constructed on top of what she heard.

options.text: A stage in which children over-apply rules until their memory for particular words matures.
options.why: A real developmental account, and one about why the error fades. The instructor's point was about what its presence shows now, rather than about when it goes away.

options.text: Interference from the regular verbs she happens to have learned most recently.
options.why: Recency is not invoked. The claim is stronger and simpler: the form was generated rather than retrieved from anywhere.

items.stem: The chapter claims these disciplines "differ less in what they study than in which question they ask about it." In a short paragraph, explain what that claim means, and say why it makes integration rather than ranking the right relationship among the fields.
items.answer: The claim is that the eight disciplines are not divided by subject matter. All of them study minds; a neuroscientist tracing how a voice becomes a person and an anthropologist asking which vocal differences a community has learned to hear are looking at one and the same moment. What separates them is the question each brings to it — how the machinery works, what operations it performs, how the capacity was built over deep time, whether the description is even well posed. Ranking the fields would require that one of those questions be the real one and the rest stand in for it until it is answered, and that is what fails. An account of the physical machinery does not contain an answer to what the machinery is for, and a description of the operation performed does not say what carries it out. Because each field is answering something the others need answered, the fields are related as parts of one explanation rather than as rivals for the same job, which is what integration means here.
rubric: States that the disciplines share their subject — all of them study minds.
Says that what distinguishes them is the question asked, and gives at least two disciplines' questions.
Explains why ranking fails: no one of these questions contains the answers to the others.
Says that each field answers something the others need, or otherwise gives the dependence a direction.
Characterizes integration as the fields forming parts of one explanation rather than competing for one job.
